{{Short description|Integral using products instead of sums}}
{{distinguish|Volterra integral equation}}
A '''product integral''' is any [[Product (mathematics)|product]]-based counterpart of the usual [[Summation|sum]]-based [[integral]] of [[calculus]]. The product integral was developed by the mathematician [[Vito Volterra]] in 1887 to solve systems of [[linear differential equation]]s.<ref>{{cite book |last1= Volterra |first1= 
V. |last2= Hostinský |first2= B. |date= 1938 |title= Opérations Infinitésimales Linéaires |language= fr |trans-title= Linear Infinitesimal Operations |publisher= Gauthier-Villars |location= Paris }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last= Slavík |first= Antonín |date= 2007 |title= Product Integration, its History and Applications |type= Dissertation |publisher= Matfyzpress |location= Prague |isbn= 80-7378-006-2 |url= http://www.karlin.mff.cuni.cz/~slavik/product/product_integration.pdf |page= 1}}</ref>

==Informal sketch==
The classical [[Riemann integral]] of a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}</math> can be defined by the relation
<math display="block">\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{\Delta x\to 0}\sum f(x_i)\,\Delta x,</math>
where the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] is taken over all [[Partition of an interval|partitions]] of the [[Interval (mathematics)|interval]] <math>[a,b]</math> whose [[Partition of an interval#Norm of a partition|norms]] approach zero. Product integrals are similar, but take the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of a [[Product (mathematics)|product]] instead of the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of a [[Summation|sum]]. They can be thought of as "[[Mathematical analysis|continuous]]" versions of "[[Discrete mathematics|discrete]]" [[Product (mathematics)|products]]. They are defined as
<math display="block">\prod_a^b \big(1 + f(x)\,dx\big) = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \prod \big(1 + f(x_i)\,\Delta x\big).</math>

For the case of {{tmath|f:[a,b]\to\R}}, the product integral reduces exactly to the case of [[Lebesgue integration]], that is, to classical calculus. Thus, the interesting cases arise for functions <math>f:[a,b]\to A</math> where <math>A</math> is either some [[commutative algebra]], such as a finite-dimensional [[matrix field]], or if <math>A</math> is a [[non-commutative algebra]]. The theories for these two cases, the commutative and non-commutative cases, have little in common. The non-commutative case is far more complicated; it requires proper [[path-ordering]] to make the integral well-defined.

===Commutative case===
For the commutative case, three distinct definitions are commonplace in the literature, referred to as Type-I, Type-II or ''geometric'', and type-III or ''bigeometric''.<ref name=nnc/><ref name="fnc2">
Michael Grossman. [https://books.google.com/books?q=%22The+First+Nonlinear+System+of+Differential+And+Integral+Calculus%E2%80%8E%22&lr=&start=10&as_brr=3 ''The First Nonlinear System of Differential And Integral Calculus''], {{ISBN|0977117006}}, 1979.</ref><ref name=bc>Michael Grossman. [https://books.google.com/books?lr=&as_brr=3&q=Bigeometric+Calculus%3A+A+System+With+a+Scale-free+Derivative%E2%80%8E&btnG=Search+Books ''Bigeometric Calculus: A System with a Scale-Free Derivative''], {{ISBN|0977117030}}, 1983.
</ref>
Such integrals have found use in [[epidemiology]] (the [[Kaplan–Meier estimator]]) and stochastic [[population dynamics]]. The geometric integral, together with the geometric derivative,  is useful in [[image analysis]]<ref name=FvA>
Luc Florack and Hans van Assen.[https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs10851-011-0275-1 "Multiplicative calculus in biomedical image analysis"], Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision, {{doi|10.1007/s10851-011-0275-1}}, 2011.
</ref> and in the study of growth/decay phenomena (''e.g.'', in [[economic growth]], [[bacterial growth]], and [[radioactive decay]]).<ref>
Diana Andrada Filip and Cyrille Piatecki. [https://halshs.archives-ouvertes.fr/file/index/docid/945788/filename/nncam.pdf "An overview on non-Newtonian calculus and its potential applications to economics"], Applied Mathematics – A Journal of Chinese Universities, Volume 28, China Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics, Springer, 2014.
</ref><ref name=model>
Agamirza E. Bashirov, Emine Misirli, Yucel Tandogdu, and Ali Ozyapici.[https://doi.org/10.1007%2Fs11766-011-2767-6 "On modelling with multiplicative differential equations"], Applied Mathematics – A Journal of Chinese Universities, Volume 26, Number 4, pages 425–428, {{doi|10.1007/s11766-011-2767-6}}, Springer, 2011.
</ref> The [[#Type III: Bigeometric integral|bigeometric integral]], together with the bigeometric derivative, is useful in some applications of [[fractals]],<ref>Marek Rybaczuk.[http://www.actabio.pwr.wroc.pl/Vol1No1/1.pdf "Critical growth of fractal patterns in biological systems"], Acta of Bioengineering and Biomechanics, Volume 1, Number 1, Wroclaw University of Technology, 1999.</ref><ref name="dimension">Marek Rybaczuk, Alicja Kedzia and Witold Zielinski (2001) [http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0960077900002319 "The concept of physical and fractal dimension II. The differential calculus in dimensional spaces"], ''Chaos, Solitons, & Fractals''Volume 12, Issue 13, October 2001, pages 2537–2552.
</ref><ref name=runge>
{{cite journal|first=Dorota|last=Aniszewska|title=Multiplicative Runge–Kutta methods|journal=[[Nonlinear Dynamics (journal)|Nonlinear Dynamics]]|volume=50|issue=1–2|date= October 2007|pages=265–272|doi=10.1007/s11071-006-9156-3|bibcode=2007NonDy..50..265A |s2cid=120404112 }}
</ref><ref>
Dorota Aniszewska and Marek Rybaczuk (2005) [http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0960077904006319 "Analysis of the multiplicative Lorenz system"], ''Chaos, Solitons & Fractals''
Volume 25, Issue 1, July 2005, pages 79–90.
</ref> and in the theory of [[Elasticity of a function|elasticity]] in economics.<ref name=nnc/><ref name=bc/><ref>
Fernando Córdova-Lepe. [http://www.bligoo.com/media/users/2/107422/files/14723/T-MAT.pdf "The multiplicative derivative as a measure of elasticity in economics"], TMAT Revista Latinoamericana de Ciencias e Ingeniería, Volume 2, Number 3, 2006.
</ref>

===Non-commutative case===
The non-commutative case commonly arises in [[quantum mechanics]] and [[quantum field theory]]. The integrand is generally an operator belonging to some [[non-commutative algebra]]. In this case, one must be careful to establish a [[path-ordering]] while integrating. A typical result is the [[ordered exponential]]. The [[Magnus expansion]] provides one technique for computing the Volterra integral. Examples include the [[Dyson expansion]], the integrals that occur in the [[operator product expansion]] and the [[Wilson line]], a product integral over a gauge field. The [[Wilson loop]] is the trace of a Wilson line. The product integral also occurs in [[control theory]], as the [[Peano–Baker series]] describing state transitions in [[linear system]]s written in a [[master equation]] type form.

==General (non-commutative) case==
The Volterra product integral is most useful when applied to matrix-valued functions or functions with values in a [[Banach algebra]]. When applied to scalars belonging to a non-commutative field, to matrixes, and to operators, i.e. to mathematical objects that do not commute, the Volterra integral splits in two definitions.<ref name="WilsonLines">{{cite book |title= Wilson Lines in Quantum Field Theory |first1= Igor Olegovich |last1= Cherednikov |first2= Tom |last2= Mertens |first3= Frederik |last3= Van der Veken |date= 2 December 2019 |publisher= Walter de Gruyter |isbn= 9783110651690 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=hUDEDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA64 }}</ref>

The '''left product integral''' is
<math display="block">P(A,D)=\prod_{i=m}^{1}(\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_i)\Delta t_i) = (\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_m)\Delta t_m) \cdots (\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_1)\Delta t_1).</math>
With this notation of left products (i.e. normal products applied from left),
<math display="block">\prod_a^b (\mathbb{1}+A(t)dt)=\lim_{\max \Delta t_i \to 0} P(A,D).</math>

The '''right product integral''' is
<math display="block">P(A,D)^*=\prod_{i=1}^{m}(\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_i)\Delta t_i) = (\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_1)\Delta t_1) \cdots (\mathbb{1}+A(\xi_m)\Delta t_m).</math>
With this notation of right products (i.e. applied from right),
<math display="block">(\mathbb{1}+A(t)dt) \prod_a^b =\lim_{\max \Delta t_i \to 0} P(A,D)^*,</math>
where <math>\mathbb{1}</math> is the [[identity matrix]] and {{tmath|D}} is a partition of the interval {{tmath|[a,b]}} in the Riemann sense, i.e. the limit is over the maximum interval in the partition. Note how in this case [[time ordering]] becomes evident in the definitions.

The [[Magnus expansion]] provides a technique for computing the product integral. It defines a continuous-time version of the [[Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula]].

The product integral satisfies a collection of properties defining a one-parameter [[continuous group]]; these are stated in two articles showing applications: the [[Dyson series]] and the [[Peano–Baker series]].

==Commutative case==
The commutative case is vastly simpler, and, as a result, a large variety of distinct notations and definitions have appeared. Three distinct styles are popular in the literature. This subsection adopts the product <math>\textstyle \prod</math> notation for product integration instead of the integral <math>\textstyle \int</math> (usually modified by a superimposed times symbol or letter 'P') favoured by [[Vito Volterra|Volterra]] and others. An arbitrary classification of types is adopted to impose some order in the field.

When the function to be integrated is valued in the real numbers, then the theory reduces exactly to the theory of [[Lebesgue integration]].

===Type I: Volterra integral===

The type I product integral corresponds to [[Vito Volterra|Volterra]]'s original definition.{{sfnp|Slavík|2007}}{{page needed|date=June 2026}}<ref name=dollardfriedman>{{cite book |first1=J. D. |last1=Dollard |first2=C. N. |last2=Friedman |title=Product integration with applications to differential equations |publisher=Addison Wesley |date=1979 |isbn=0-201-13509-4 }}</ref><ref name=gantmacher>{{cite book |first=F. R. |last=Gantmacher |date=1959 |title=The Theory of Matrices |volume=1 and 2 }}</ref> The following relationship exists for [[scalar function]]s {{tmath| f:[a,b] \to \mathbb{R} }}:
<math display="block">\prod_a^b \big(1 + f(x)\,dx\big) = \exp\left(\int_a^b f(x) \,dx\right).</math>

===Type II: Geometric integral===
<math display="block">\prod_a^b f(x)^{dx} = \lim_{\Delta x \to 0} \prod{f(x_i)^{\Delta x}} = \exp\left(\int_a^b \ln f(x) \,dx\right),</math>
which is called the '''geometric integral'''. The logarithm is well-defined if {{tmath|f}} takes values in the real or [[Complex number|complex numbers]], or if {{tmath|f}} takes values in a commutative field of commuting [[trace-class]] operators. This definition of the product integral is the [[Mathematical analysis|continuous]] analog of the [[Discrete mathematics|discrete]] [[Product (mathematics)|product]] [[Functional (mathematics)|operator]] <math>\textstyle \prod_{i=a}^b</math> (with {{tmath|i, a, b \in \mathbb{Z} }}) and the [[Multiplicative function|multiplicative]] analog to the (normal/standard/[[Additive map|additive]]) [[integral]] <math>\textstyle \int_a^b dx</math> (with {{tmath| x \in [a,b] }}):

{| class="wikitable plainrowheaders"
|+ Discrete and continuous additive and multiplicative operators
|-
! scope="col" | Type
! scope="col" | [[Additive map|additive]]
! scope="col" | [[Completely multiplicative function|multiplicative]]
|-
! [[Discrete mathematics|discrete]]
| <math>\sum_{i=a}^b f(i)</math> || <math>\prod_{i=a}^b f(i)</math>
|-
! [[Mathematical analysis|continuous]]
|<math>\int_a^b f(x)\,dx</math>||<math>\prod_a^b f(x)^{dx}</math>
|}

It is very useful in [[Probability theory|stochastics]], where the [[Likelihood function#Log-likelihood|log-likelihood]] (i.e. the [[logarithm]] of a product integral of [[Independence (probability theory)|independent]] [[random variable]]s) equals the [[integral]] of the [[logarithm]] of these ([[infinitesimal]]ly many) [[random variable]]s:
<math display="block">\ln \prod_a^b p(x)^{dx} = \int_a^b \ln p(x) \,dx.</math>

===Type III: Bigeometric integral===
<math display="block">\prod_a^b f(x)^{d(\ln x)} = \exp\left(\int_{\ln(a)}^{\ln(b)} \ln f(e^x) \,dx\right),</math>
The type III product integral is called the '''bigeometric integral'''.

===Basic results===
For the commutative case, the following results hold for the type II product integral (the geometric integral). 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\prod_a^b c^{dx} &= c^{b-a}, \\
\prod_a^b x^{dx} &= \frac{b^b}{a^a} {\rm e}^{a-b}, \\
\prod_0^b x^{dx} &= b^b {\rm e}^{-b},
\end{align}</math>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\prod_a^b \left(f(x)^k\right)^{dx} &= \left(\prod_a^b f(x)^{dx}\right)^k, \\
\prod_a^b \left(c^{f(x)}\right)^{dx} &= c^{\int_a^b f(x) \,dx}.
\end{align}</math>

The geometric integral (type II above) plays a central role in the '''geometric calculus''',<ref name=nnc>
M. Grossman, R. Katz, [https://books.google.com/books?q=%22Non-Newtonian+Calculus%22&btnG=Search+Books, ''Non-Newtonian Calculus''], {{isbn|0-912938-01-3}}, Lee Press, 1972.
</ref><ref name=fnc2/><ref>A. E. Bashirov, E. M. Kurpınar, A. Özyapıcı. [http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022247X07003824 ''Multiplicative calculus and its applications''], Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications, 2008.</ref> which is a multiplicative calculus. The inverse of the geometric integral, which is the '''geometric derivative''', denoted {{tmath| f^*(x) }}, is defined using the following relationship:
<math display="block">f^*(x)=\exp\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\right).</math>

For {{tmath|X}} is a [[random variable]] with [[Probability distribution#Cumulative distribution function|probability distribution]] {{tmath| F(x)}}, the following can be concluded:
{{glossary begin}}
{{term| Fundamental theorem of calculus }}
{{defn| {{gmain|Fundamental theorem of calculus}}
<math display="block">\prod_a^b f^*(x)^{dx} = \prod_a^b \exp\left(\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \,dx\right) = \frac{f(b)}{f(a)},</math>
}}

{{term| Product rule }}
{{defn| {{gmain|Product rule}}
<math display="block">(fg)^* = f^* g^*.</math>
}}

{{term| Quotient rule }}
{{defn| {{gmain|Quotient rule}}
<math display="block">(f/g)^* = f^*/g^*.</math>
}}

{{term| Law of large numbers }}
{{defn| {{gmain|Law of large numbers}}
<math display="block">\sqrt[n]{X_1 X_2 \cdots X_n} \underset{n \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \prod_x X^{dF(x)}.</math>
}}
{{glossary end}}

Compare with the standard [[law of large numbers]]:
<math display="block">\frac{X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n}{n} \underset{n \to \infty}{\longrightarrow} \int X \,dF(x).</math>

==Commutative case: Lebesgue-type product-integrals==
When the integrand takes values in the [[real number]]s, then the product intervals become easy to work with by using [[simple function]]s. Just as in the case of [[Lebesgue integration|Lebesgue version of (classical) integrals]], one can compute product integrals by approximating them with the product integrals of [[simple function]]s. The case of Type II geometric integrals reduces to exactly the case of classical Lebesgue integration.

===Type I: Volterra integral===

Because [[simple function]]s generalize [[step function]]s, in what follows we will only consider the special case of simple functions that are step functions. This will also make it easier to compare the [[Lebesgue integration|Lebesgue definition]] with the [[Riemann integral|Riemann definition]].

Given a step function <math>f: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}</math> with a [[Partition of an interval#Tagged partitions|tagged partition]]
<math display="block">a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b, \quad x_0 \le t_1 \le x_1, x_1 \le t_2 \le x_2, \dots, x_{n-1} \le t_n \le x_n,</math>
one [[Approximation#Mathematics|approximation]] of the "Riemann definition" of the [[#Type I: Volterra integral|type I product integral]] is given by{{sfnp|Slavík|2007|p=65}}
<math display="block">\prod_{k=1}^n \left[ \big(1 + f(t_k)\big) \cdot (x_k - x_{k-1}) \right].</math>

The (type I) product integral was defined to be, roughly speaking, the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] of these products by [[Ludwig Schlesinger]] in a 1931 article.{{which|date=May 2018}}

Another approximation of the "Riemann definition" of the Type I product integral is defined as
<math display="block">\prod_{k=1}^n \exp\big(f(t_k) \cdot (x_k - x_{k-1})\big).</math>

When <math>f</math> is a [[constant function]], the limit of the first type of approximation is equal to the second type of approximation.{{sfnp|Slavík|2007|p=71}} Notice that in general, for a step function, the value of the second type of approximation does not depend on the partition, as long as the partition is a [[Partition of an interval#Refinement of a partition|refinement]] of the partition defining the step function, whereas the value of the first type of approximation {{em|does}} depend on the fineness of the partition, even when it is a refinement of the partition defining the step function.

It turns out that{{sfnp|Slavík|2007|p=72}} for {{em|any}} product-integrable function {{tmath|f}}, the limit of the first type of approximation equals the limit of the second type of approximation. Since, for step functions, the value of the second type of approximation doesn't depend on the fineness of the partition for partitions "fine enough", it makes sense to define{{sfnp|Slavík|2007|p=80}} the "Lebesgue (type I) product integral" of a step function as
<math display="block">\prod_a^b \big(1 + f(x) \,dx\big) \overset{def}{=} \prod_{k=1}^n \exp\big(f(s_k) \cdot (y_k - y_{k-1})\big),</math>
where {{tmath|1= y_0 < a = s_1 <}} {{tmath|y_1 < \dots < y_{n-1} <}} {{tmath|1= s_n < y_n = b}} is the tagged partition corresponding to the step function {{tmath|f}}. (In contrast, the corresponding quantity would not be unambiguously defined using the first type of approximation.)

This generalizes to arbitrary [[measure space]]s readily. If <math>X</math> is a measure space with [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]] {{tmath|\mu}}, then for any product-integrable simple function <math>f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k I_{A_k}(x)</math> (i.e. a [[conical combination]] of the [[indicator function]]s for some [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] measurable sets {{tmath| A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n \subseteq X }}), its type I product integral is defined to be
<math display="block">\prod_X \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \overset{def}{=} \prod_{k=1}^n \exp\big(a_k \mu(A_k)\big),</math>
since {{tmath|a_k}} is the value of {{tmath|f}} at any point of {{tmath|A_k}}. In the special case where {{tmath|1= X = \mathbb{R} }}, {{tmath|\mu}} is [[Lebesgue measure]], and all of the measurable sets {{tmath|A_k}} are [[Interval (mathematics)|intervals]], one can verify that this is equal to the definition given above for that special case. Analogous to [[Lebesgue integration|the theory of Lebesgue (classical) integrals]], the Type I product integral of any product-integrable function {{tmath|f}} can be written as the limit of an increasing [[sequence]] of Volterra product integrals of product-integrable simple functions.

Taking [[logarithm]]s of both sides of the above definition, one gets that for any product-integrable simple function {{tmath|f}}:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \ln \left(\prod_X \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \right) = \ln \left( \prod_{k=1}^n \exp\big(a_k \mu(A_k)\big) \right) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k \mu(A_k) = \int_X f(x) \,d\mu(x) \\
& \quad\iff \prod_X \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) = \exp \left( \int_X f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right),
\end{align}</math>
where we used the definition of integral for simple functions. Moreover, because [[continuous function]]s like <math>\exp</math> can be interchanged with limits, and the product integral of any product-integrable function <math>f</math> is equal to the limit of product integrals of simple functions, it follows that the relationship
<math display="block">\prod_X \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) = \exp \left( \int_X f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right)</math>
holds generally for {{em|any}} product-integrable {{tmath|f}}. This clearly generalizes the property mentioned above.

The Type I integral is multiplicative as a [[set function]],<ref>Gill, Richard D., Soren Johansen. [https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~jordan/sail/readings/gill-johansen.pdf "A Survey of Product Integration with a View Toward Application in Survival Analysis"]. The Annals of Statistics 18, no. 4 (December 1990): 1501—555, p. 1503.</ref> which can be shown using the above property. More specifically, given a product-integrable function <math>f</math> one can define a set function <math>{\cal V}_f</math> by defining, for every measurable set {{tmath|B \subseteq X}},
<math display="block">{\cal V}_f(B) \overset{def}{=} \prod_B \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \overset{def}{=} \prod_X \big(1 + (f \cdot I_B)(x) \,d\mu(x)\big),</math>
where <math>I_B(x)</math> denotes the [[indicator function]] of {{tmath|B}}. Then for any two ''disjoint'' measurable sets <math>B_1, B_2</math> one has
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 {\cal V}_f(B_1 \sqcup B_2) &= \prod_{B_1 \sqcup B_2} \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \\
 &= \exp\left( \int_{B_1 \sqcup B_2} f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right) \\
 &= \exp\left( \int_{B_1} f(x) \,d\mu(x) + \int_{B_2} f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right) \\
 &= \exp\left( \int_{B_1} f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right) \exp\left( \int_{B_2} f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right) \\
 &= \prod_{B_1} (1 + f(x)d \mu(x)) \prod_{ B_2} (1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)) \\
 &= {\cal V}_f(B_1 ) {\cal V}_f(B_2).
\end{align}</math>

This property can be contrasted with measures, which are [[sigma-additive]] [[set function]]s.

However, the Type I integral is {{em|not}} [[Multiplicative function|multiplicative]] as a [[Functional (mathematics)|functional]]. Given two product-integrable functions {{tmath|f,g}}, and a measurable set {{tmath|A}}, it is generally the case that
<math display="block">\prod_A \big(1 + (fg)(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \neq \prod_A \big(1 + f(x) \,d\mu(x)\big) \prod_A \big(1 + g(x) \,d\mu(x)\big).</math>

===Type II: Geometric integral===

If <math>X</math> is a measure space with measure {{tmath|\mu}}, then for any product-integrable simple function <math>f(x) = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k I_{A_k}(x)</math> (i.e. a [[conical combination]] of the [[indicator function]]s for some disjoint measurable sets {{tmath| A_1, A_2, \dots, A_n \subseteq X }}), its type II product integral is defined to be
<math display="block">\prod_X f(x)^{d\mu(x)} \overset{def}{=} \prod_{k=1}^n a_k^{\mu(A_k)}.</math>

This can be seen to generalize the definition given above.

Taking logarithms of both sides, we see that for any product-integrable simple function {{tmath|f}}:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
& \ln \left( \prod_X f(x)^{d\mu(x)} \right) = \sum_{k=1}^n \ln(a_k) \mu(A_k) = \int_X \ln f(x) \,d\mu (x) \\
& \quad \iff \prod_X f(x)^{d\mu(x)} = \exp\left( \int_X \ln f(x) \,d\mu (x) \right),
\end{align}</math>
where the definition of the Lebesgue integral for simple functions was used. This observation, analogous to the one already made for Type II integrals above, allows one to entirely reduce the "Lebesgue theory of type II geometric integrals" to the Lebesgue theory of (classical) integrals. In other words, because continuous functions like <math>\exp</math> and <math>\ln</math> can be interchanged with limits, and the product integral of any product-integrable function <math>f</math> is equal to the limit of some increasing sequence of product integrals of simple functions, it follows that the relationship
<math display="block">\prod_X f(x)^{d\mu(x)} = \exp\left( \int_X \ln f(x) \,d\mu(x) \right)</math>
holds generally for {{em|any}} product-integrable {{tmath|f}}. This generalizes the property of geometric integrals mentioned above.
